transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. It’s... it’s actually really difficult for me to be sitting in this chair. You see, being a psychologist myself, I’m usually the one on the other side of this dynamic, analyzing the thought processes and the behavioral patterns. So to be the one coming in as the patient... it’s a lot to process. But I had to come in because... well, things are happening that I just can't rationalize away anymore. 

I keep hearing Garrett’s voice. And I don't mean like an echo of a memory or my own internal monologue, I mean I hear him as clearly as if he is standing right directly behind me. It’s been happening a lot when I’m out walking on the trail—there's this specific dirt trail I go to where it's usually very quiet and isolated—or I'll be at home, just standing in my painting room, completely focused on mixing colors on the palette, and suddenly his voice is just... right there in the room with me. 

And the most distressing part of all of this, the thing that really drove me to finally make this appointment, is that a part of me—the clinical, logical part of my brain—knows that Garrett is dead. I know he is gone. But in the exact moment when it happens, when he speaks to me, it feels completely, undeniably real. I can hear the exact timbre of his voice, the way he breathes between words, and I catch myself actually turning around to answer him because my brain just fully accepts that he's standing right there. It’s... it's exhausting, honestly, to experience something so vivid when you know it shouldn't be possible.
Do you hear Garrett's voice at any other times besides when you're on the trail or in your painting room?

Well, no, it’s mostly just those two places, but... the timing of it is really what’s significant here, and I think it’s important to give you the full context because, as a clinician, I know how crucial the timeline is for differential diagnosis. 

You see, the voice—hearing Garrett like that—it didn’t start right after he passed. It wasn’t part of the initial acute bereavement phase. I know what ordinary grief looks like, I know what it feels like, and this wasn’t that. This didn't start until... well, until I had this massive shift. It was this prolonged stretch where I was just completely, undeniably wired. I mean, my energy levels were off the charts. I was barely sleeping—maybe an hour or two a night, if that—and I didn't even feel tired. I actually felt like I was operating at a higher frequency than everyone else. 

During that time, I was taking on these massive, frankly impossible projects. I decided I was going to completely remodel the entire first floor of my house by myself, while simultaneously trying to write a book on cognitive behavioral interventions that I hadn't even outlined yet. I just felt this intense, relentless drive to keep going, keep moving, keep producing. And it was right in the middle of all that—that intense, elevated state—that I first heard him. I had never experienced anything remotely like it before that mood shifted so drastically. It’s like my brain just went into overdrive and suddenly, there he was.
How long did this intense, elevated state with high energy levels and reduced sleep last?

Well, the timeline of this whole thing is... it's actually quite striking when you look at it from a clinical perspective, which is what I keep trying to do to maintain some semblance of control over the situation. But, to answer your question directly—though I think the context of how it all unfolded is just as important—this entire crisis, this whole unraveling of my normal cognitive baseline, has been going on for about a month. 

Exactly a month, actually, since Garrett died. I remember the timeline so clearly because it was almost immediately after the funeral that the shift happened. I didn't have that typical period of lethargy or profound sadness that you'd expect. Instead, I just catapulted into this state of absolute, boundless energy. So, for the past four weeks—a full month—I've been in this relentless, elevated state. And it hasn't let up. The sleeplessness, the projects, the racing thoughts, and then, of course, the auditory hallucinations... it's all been packed into this one, incredibly dense, exhausting month since he passed. It feels like a lifetime, honestly, but on the calendar, it's been just about four weeks of this continuous, high-octane crisis.
Do you hear Garrett's voice when you're feeling calm or is it usually when you're under stress or experiencing strong emotions?

Well, that’s... that’s a really fascinating question, actually, because you would think—from a strictly theoretical standpoint—that hallucinations triggered by bereavement would be highly correlated with moments of acute emotional distress or anxiety. You’d expect them to happen when the psyche is overwhelmed. But the reality of my experience... it completely defies that expectation. 

It’s not when I’m stressed. It’s not when I’m having a breakdown or crying or feeling overwhelmed by the grief. In fact, it’s almost the exact opposite. Like I mentioned, it happens when I’m out on that dirt trail, walking. And when I’m out there, I’m not ruminating on his death or feeling anxious; I’m actually just feeling this incredible, buzzing energy. I’m walking fast, my mind is racing with all these brilliant ideas for my book, and I feel completely invigorated. Or when I’m in the painting room—I’m not sad when I’m painting. I’m hyper-focused, completely dialed into the colors and the canvas, feeling this absolute mastery over what I’m doing. 

So it’s not stress in the traditional sense, and it’s certainly not sadness. It’s... it’s happening right in the middle of this intense, elevated drive. I’m feeling fantastic, powerful even, and then—bam—there’s his voice, clear as day, right behind me. It’s so counterintuitive, which is why I’ve been trying so hard to analyze it, to figure out the exact trigger, but it just doesn’t map onto the typical stress-response model at all. It’s just tied to this... this relentless high I’ve been riding.
Do you ever question whether the voice you hear is actually Garrett's or if it's just your mind playing a trick on you?

That is exactly the crux of the issue, isn't it? It’s the cognitive dissonance of the whole experience that really drove me to seek help, because... well, logically, rationally, my clinical brain knows he’s gone. I stood at his grave. I know he is dead. I know that dead people do not speak. So, yes, there is a part of me—the psychologist part, the rational adult part—that questions it, that tries to tell me, "This is a hallucination, this is your mind playing an elaborate trick on you." 

But... and this is the part that’s so terrifying and so utterly convincing... when it happens, when I’m out on that trail or standing in the painting room, it doesn't feel like a trick. It doesn't feel like a memory or an internal monologue. I hear his voice as clearly as if he is standing right behind me. The timbre, the cadence, the exact way he used to say my name—it is perfectly replicated. In that split second, the reality of his death just vanishes, and it feels completely, undeniably real. I even turn around, expecting to see him. I mean, I physically turn my body because my brain is processing the auditory input as a genuine external stimulus. And then, of course, there's no one there. And the crash of realizing that, the whiplash between knowing he's dead and experiencing his voice so vividly... it’s just exhausting. That's why I came in, honestly. Because knowing it isn't real doesn't make it feel any less real when it's happening, if that makes any sense.
Have you experienced any hallucinations other than hearing Garrett's voice, such as seeing or feeling things that aren't there?

Well, no, not seeing or feeling things. No visual anomalies, no tactile hallucinations—none of that. It’s strictly auditory, and strictly him. Which, again, is why I came in to see you in the first place, because it’s just this one very specific, very intense phenomenon. I keep hearing Garrett’s voice, and only his voice. 

And like I was saying, it’s not a vague whisper or some indistinct mumbling that I could easily brush off as the wind or my imagination. It’s as clearly as if he’s standing right behind me. It happens on that dirt trail, it happens in my painting room... and the clarity of it is just astonishing. I mean, even though part of me—the educated, rational part—knows he’s dead, in the moment it happens, it feels completely, undeniably real. It’s so real that it overrides my logic entirely. I don't see him, I don't feel a hand on my shoulder or anything like that, but the sound of his voice is so perfectly rendered in my environment that I don't need to see him to believe he's there for that split second. It’s just the voice. But that alone is enough to completely shatter my reality, which is why I’m sitting in this chair talking to you.
Are you feeling any specific emotions when you hear Garrett's voice, such as happiness, sadness, or anxiety?

Well, that’s the thing, it’s not the emotions you’d typically associate with grief. It’s not sadness, and it’s definitely not anxiety. Like I was trying to explain earlier, the emotional state I’m in when I hear him is... it's this intense, electric drive. I only started hearing Garrett’s voice during this incredibly wired stretch I’ve been in. This period where I barely sleep—maybe a couple of hours a night, if that—and yet I have the energy to take on these massive, impossible projects, like writing an entire book or painting for hours on end without a break. 

I feel this relentless compulsion to just keep going, keep producing, keep moving. And it’s right in the middle of that—when I’m feeling the most energized, the most driven, almost euphoric with how much I can accomplish—that’s when his voice cuts through. I had never, ever heard him like that before this whole mood shift started. I mean, after he died, I went through ordinary grief. I was devastated, I was crying, I was mourning him in the way you’d expect. But I never heard his voice then. Not once. It wasn’t until this... this high kicked in, this period of just being completely unstoppable and hyper-focused, that the auditory phenomenon began. So the emotion isn’t sadness or fear; it’s this overwhelming, vibrating energy. It’s all tied to this specific, elevated state I’ve been in, which just makes the whole thing even more perplexing from a psychological standpoint.
Do you think the voice you hear is trying to communicate something specific to you or is it just random?

You know, it’s funny you ask that, because given my background, my immediate instinct was to look for the underlying meaning, right? The symbolism of it all. If my mind is going to the incredible effort of projecting a voice this vivid, this perfectly rendered, you’d think it would have some profound message. You’d think it would be like... I don't know, some cinematic moment where he tells me he's at peace, or gives me some grand life advice. 

But... no. There's really no specific message at all. It's not like he's trying to communicate some hidden truth or warn me about anything. It's usually just... mundane. It's just my name. Just him saying, 'Hey,' or sometimes just a fragment of a sentence that completely trails off before I can even grasp what the context might have been. It feels completely random. Which, honestly, is almost more frustrating in a way, because if he were saying something profound, maybe I could analyze it. Maybe I could tell myself, 'Ah, this is just my psyche processing unresolved grief.' But there's no narrative structure to it. It’s just this... this misfire. 

And yet, because I’m in this state right now—this incredibly elevated, buzzing, electric state where my mind is constantly connecting dots and I'm churning out work for hours on end—I catch myself trying to decode it anyway. I’ll stop dead in my tracks in the painting room and think, 'Why did he say my name with exactly that inflection? What does it mean?' I'll spend twenty minutes just spinning my wheels on it, analyzing a single syllable. But at the end of the day, no, there's no specific communication. It's just the random firing of a brain that's currently running on absolute overdrive, projecting the most familiar voice it knows into the empty space of the room. It’s just random.
Have you experienced any periods where the voice of Garrett stopped for a significant amount of time since it first started?

Well, no, not really. I mean, not since this whole... this whole hyper-energized phase started. It hasn't stopped for any meaningful stretch of time at all. It’s been remarkably consistent, which is part of what’s so fascinating—and exhausting—about it. I mean, you’d think, logically, that an auditory hallucination would wax and wane, right? That maybe there would be a day or two where my brain just sort of rests and the projection stops. But that hasn't happened. 

Since the very first time I heard him on the trail—which, again, coincided perfectly with this sudden surge of energy and this inability to sleep—it’s been a daily occurrence. Sometimes it’s just once a day, maybe right when I’m getting into the zone with my painting or when I’m furiously typing away at my manuscript at three in the morning. Other times, it might happen two or three times in a single afternoon. But there hasn't been a significant gap. There hasn't been a full 24 or 48 hours where I can say, 'Ah, okay, Garrett’s quiet today.' 

And because I’m so keyed up right now, because my mind is just racing constantly, I’m hyper-aware of it. I’m almost waiting for it, in a way. I’ll be in the middle of a thought, connecting all these brilliant ideas for my book, and then—bam—there’s the voice. And then I’m off on a tangent, analyzing why it happened at that exact second. So, no, there haven’t been any real breaks. It’s just this continuous, unpredictable, but daily interruption in the middle of this massive creative output I’m experiencing. It’s always there, just waiting to pop up.
Do you think your mood or emotional state changes immediately before or after you hear Garrett's voice?

Well, it’s... it’s interesting you ask about the immediate before and after, because the baseline right now is already so intense, right? I’m already operating on this incredibly high frequency. But, yes, there is a shift, or at least there was a very distinct pattern when this all first started. 

Right before I hear him, or maybe exactly as it happens, there’s this... this feeling of being almost lit up from the inside. It’s hard to describe accurately, even with my background, but it’s like I suddenly have this urgent, undeniable purpose. It’s this profound sense of clarity and drive, like I’m tapped into something massive that no one else can see or understand. I’ll be standing there, maybe staring at a canvas or pacing the floor, and I just feel this electric surge of importance. And then the voice happens. 

But the aftermath... that’s where it gets complicated. Because I’m in this state of absolute, buzzing purpose, if anyone—and I mean anyone—interrupts me right after, or questions what I’m doing, or tries to slow my momentum... I just snap. It’s not just annoyance; it’s this immediate, blinding rage. Like, how dare they interrupt this critical work? How dare they not see how important this is? 

I remember a few days ago, I had just heard him say my name while I was reorganizing my entire library by thematic resonance—which is a massive undertaking, by the way, requiring total concentration—and my neighbor knocked on the door to ask about a misdelivered package. Just a normal, mundane thing. But I opened the door and just laid into him. I was furious. I felt this incredible hostility because he was breaking my focus, slowing down this incredible, lit-up momentum I had going. So, the mood shifts from this euphoric, urgent purpose right into this razor-sharp irritability if the outside world tries to intrude on it. It’s like a pendulum swinging from absolute brilliance to total fury in a matter of seconds.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this where you felt extremely energetic, irritable, or unusually happy for an extended time?

Well, you know, it's... I don't think so. Not like this. I mean, as a psychologist, I've spent a lot of time analyzing my own baseline, right? You have to, in this field. You have to know your own emotional topography so you don't project onto your clients. And generally speaking, I’ve always considered myself a fairly driven person. I have a good work ethic, I get things done, I enjoy my research. But this? This level of sheer, unadulterated electricity running through my veins? No. 

I mean, sure, I’ve had times where I felt good about a project, maybe stayed up late a couple of nights to finish a paper because I was in the flow state. But that was always tied to a specific external stimulus, a specific deadline, and it had a clear beginning and end. It was manageable. I still needed sleep eventually. I still felt tired. 

What I'm experiencing right now is entirely different. It's not just being happy or energetic; it's this... this expansive, boundless state where sleep feels not just unnecessary, but almost like an insult to my potential. And the irritability—that sudden, blinding rage when someone interrupts me—that is definitely new. I’ve always been a pretty patient guy. You have to be, sitting in a chair listening to people's problems all day. You cultivate patience. But lately, my tolerance for anything that slows me down is absolutely zero. 

So, if you're asking if I've ever had a period like this before... no. Never. This feels entirely unprecedented in my life. It's like I've been driving a reliable sedan my whole life, and suddenly I woke up behind the wheel of a Formula One race car, and someone bricked the accelerator to the floor. I'm just trying to steer, you know? But no, before this current phase, I've never experienced anything close to this level of sustained, intense energy or this kind of explosive irritability. It's all completely new territory for me.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or experienced symptoms of bipolar disorder in the past?

Well, no, not officially. I mean, I’ve never sat across from someone like you and had them hand me that specific label. And it’s fascinating, really, because as a psychologist, you’d think I would have caught something like that if it were lurking in the background. We spend years studying the DSM, right? We learn the criteria, the specifiers, the exact duration of symptoms required for a diagnosis. We dissect case studies until we can practically diagnose people in our sleep. So, you’d assume that if I had any history of this... this kind of cyclical mood disturbance, I would have recognized the signs in myself. 

But looking back, analyzing my own history with the same critical eye I’d apply to a patient, there just isn’t anything there that fits the bill. I’ve never had a depressive episode, for one. I’ve never had those periods of profound lethargy or anhedonia that usually accompany a bipolar diagnosis. And as I just mentioned, I’ve certainly never had a manic or hypomanic episode before this current... whatever this is. This explosion of energy. 

I’ve always been very steady. Very even-keeled. My colleagues used to joke that I was the most predictable person in the department. I had my routine, my research, my clinical hours. I was the guy you went to when you needed a calm, rational perspective on a difficult case. There were no wild swings, no impulsive decisions, no grandiosity. Just a solid, dependable baseline. 

So, no, I’ve never been diagnosed with it, and honestly, I’ve never experienced anything that would even warrant the suspicion of it until now. Which makes this whole experience—the energy, the lack of sleep, the voice of Garrett—even more perplexing. It’s like this entirely new paradigm has just dropped into my life out of nowhere, completely overriding the psychological framework I’ve operated within for my entire adult life. It’s... it's academically fascinating, really, even as I’m the one living through it, to see how suddenly and completely the mind can shift gears without any prior history to suggest it was possible.
Have you ever had an episode like this before, where you felt extremely energetic and irritable for an extended period?

I feel like we’re treading the exact same ground here, Doctor, which I suppose is part of your diagnostic process, but as I just explained a moment ago, no. I have never had an episode like this in the past. Never. 

But if you’re asking me to break down exactly what this current state feels like again, to really get into the mechanics of the mood itself and how it operates, I can certainly elaborate on what I was just telling you. Because it really is a fascinating duality, experientially speaking. 

When this all kicked off, at first, I felt almost completely lit up. That’s really the most accurate way I can describe it—lit up from the inside out, humming with it. It was like I had suddenly been handed this incredibly urgent, monumental purpose that absolutely no one else around me could see or even begin to comprehend. I was—and am—operating on this entirely different plane of understanding. 

But the friction comes from the rest of the world, you see? Because I have this profound purpose, if anyone—and I mean literally anyone, whether it's a neighbor at the door or a colleague—if they questioned what I was doing, or if they tried to slow me down even a fraction of a second, I would just snap. It isn't just a mild annoyance; I snap into this absolute, pure rage. Because how could they not see it? How could they dare to interfere with something so obviously critical? 

So, to answer your question again, I’ve never experienced anything like this before in my entire life. This specific combination of being illuminated with purpose and then becoming instantly, explosively furious if obstructed... it is entirely unique to what is happening to me right now.
Do you think hearing Garrett's voice is a way for your mind to cope with his loss?

Intellectually? Yes. I mean, as a clinician, that is exactly the textbook explanation I would offer a patient. Bereavement hallucinations. The psyche’s desperate, fascinating attempt to bridge the gap between profound attachment and sudden, unacceptable loss. I’ve read the literature, I’ve... well, I’ve counseled people through complex grief responses. So, part of me desperately wants to neatly categorize it as exactly that—a subconscious coping mechanism, a way for my brain to buffer the shock. 

But... and this is the entire crux of why I actually came in, why I finally decided I needed to sit in this chair... the experiential reality of what is happening completely defies my clinical understanding. Because I keep hearing Garrett’s voice, and it is not some vague, internal echo of a memory. It’s not an internal monologue. I hear him as clearly as if he is standing right directly behind me. 

I’ll be out on the trail, you know, just trying to burn off some of this relentless, buzzing energy, and he'll speak. Or I'll be in my painting room. That's my sanctuary, my private space where I go to focus and create, and suddenly his voice is just... occupying the actual acoustic space of the room. The timbre of it, the pitch, the slight intake of breath he always took before he made a sarcastic comment—it’s flawless. It has spatial origin. 

And it creates this agonizing cognitive dissonance. Because the rational part of my brain—the part that spent years in grad school, the part that understands object permanence and mortality—knows he’s dead. I know he is gone. But in the moment? When that sound hits my eardrums? It feels completely, absolutely real. It doesn't feel like a coping mechanism in that split second. It feels like he is physically standing there, and my brain just accepts it as reality before my logic can even attempt to catch up. It’s terrifying, frankly, to have your own sensory input override your reality testing that completely.
Have you experienced any periods of significantly decreased need for sleep that lasted for several days before hearing Garrett's voice?

Well, that's... that's actually the sequence of events that finally pushed me to make this appointment, because the timing of it all is just so clinically significant. If I were charting this for a patient, I'd be circling the timeline in red ink, you know? Because, no, I didn't hear him before the sleep issues started. It wasn't just ordinary grief where you think you hear a key in the lock or a footstep on the stairs in the weeks right after the funeral. This was entirely different. 

The auditory hallucinations—and I know that's what they are, even if they feel entirely real in the moment—they only started during this... this wired stretch. That's really the best way to describe it. It was after I had gone several days with barely any sleep. I’m talking maybe two hours a night, if that, and yet I felt completely rested. More than rested, I felt driven. I was taking on these massive, impossible projects around the house, repainting the entire living room at 3 AM, reorganizing my entire clinical library by publication year and then by author’s theoretical orientation... just driven by this relentless, buzzing motor to keep going, keep moving, keep doing. 

And it was right in the middle of that—when I was running on fumes but felt like a nuclear reactor—that I first heard him. Clear as day. I had never heard him like that before this entire mood shift happened. It was only once the energy spiked, once the sleep dropped off a cliff, and once I was locked into this hyper-focused, irritable state that his voice actually manifested in the physical space of the room. So the sleep disruption definitely preceded the voice. It's like the lack of sleep and the energy surge somehow thinned the veil between my internal grief and my external sensory processing, allowing the hallucination to break through.
Have you experienced any periods of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted for at least one week?

Well, as for the duration, yes, absolutely. It’s been far longer than a week. If we’re looking at the entire timeline of this... this whole crisis, this entire state of being wired and irritable and just vibrating with this bizarre energy, it has been unfolding for about a month now. 

It all really started tracking back to when Garrett died. That was the catalyst, obviously. The first few days after it happened, I was just numb, which is standard, of course. But then, rather than slipping into a typical depressive mourning period, the engine just turned over and started revving. And it hasn't stopped. So for the past month, I have been locked into this elevated, agitated, completely relentless state. It's not just a passing mood swing or a couple of bad days where I felt a bit snappy. It has been a sustained, unbroken month of feeling like I am operating at a hundred and fifty percent capacity, while simultaneously being so irritable that the slightest interference makes me want to tear the walls down. 

So, yes, to answer your question about the one-week criteria, we have well and truly surpassed that. It’s been a solid four weeks of this continuous, exhausting, yet somehow exhilarating escalation since I lost him. It's fascinating, really, in a horrifying sort of way, how the mind can sustain this level of physiological and psychological arousal for an entire month without just completely short-circuiting. But here I am, thirty days in, and the motor is still running hot.
Do you feel guilty or blame yourself for Garrett's death?

Guilt? Oh, God, guilt doesn't even begin to cover it. It's... it's like this crushing, suffocating weight that I just drag around with me every single second of the day. I mean, intellectually, I know the stages of grief, I know about survivor's guilt, I know how the mind tries to find control in a situation where there was none. I could give a seminar on it. But experiencing it? It's entirely different. 

I just... I keep replaying every single interaction, every last conversation with Garrett. I analyze the tone of my voice, the words I chose, the things I didn't say. Did I tell him I loved him enough that morning? Was I too distracted by work? I comb through my memories like a crime scene investigator, looking for the exact moment I failed him. And it's not just Garrett. It bleeds into everything else. I think about my patients, the ones whose sessions I've had to cancel recently because I'm in this... this state. I think about how I'm abandoning them when they need me, how I'm failing in my ethical duty as a clinician. 

It just spirals, you know? It starts with Garrett and then it just expands outward until I'm absolutely convinced that I have failed everyone who has ever relied on me. I look at the wreck I've become, this buzzing, hallucinating mess, and I genuinely, deeply believe that everyone—my patients, my colleagues, my friends—would just be so much better off if I weren't in the way. If I just... removed myself from the equation. It's this profound, inescapable sense of utter worthlessness that just sits in my chest, completely immune to any cognitive restructuring or rational thought I try to apply to it. It’s just... it’s exhausting.

Have you experienced any periods of abnormally elevated mood that lasted for at least one week and were accompanied by at least three other specific symptoms such as inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, or excessive talkativeness?

Well, we are definitely checking off the diagnostic criteria today, aren't we? But yes, to answer your question about that specific cluster of symptoms... absolutely. It wasn't just that I had energy or felt a little better. At first, I felt almost... lit up. That's the best phrase for it. Incandescent. Like my brain had been plugged directly into a high-voltage line. 

I felt like I had this urgent, profound purpose that no one else could see or even begin to comprehend. I was entirely convinced I was making these groundbreaking, visionary connections about the nature of grief and human consciousness, things that were going to completely revolutionize my clinical practice and probably the entire field of psychology. I felt untouchable, honestly. My mind was just expanding to hold all these brilliant insights, and I felt so uniquely capable, so much smarter and more dialed-in than anyone around me. 

And because I was having all these massive revelations, I couldn't stop talking about them. The words were just spilling out of me, completely unspooled and rapid-fire. I was leaving these frantic, ten-minute voicemails for my colleagues in the middle of the night—because, as we established, my need for sleep was basically zero—just talking a mile a minute about my theories, jumping from one idea to the next. 

But the flip side of that elevation... the really destructive part... was how volatile it was. If anyone didn't immediately grasp my brilliance, or if they questioned me, I would just snap into absolute rage. I mean, a blinding, terrifying level of anger. My sister came over to check on me, saw the state of the house and the manicured chaos of my library project, and gently tried to suggest I slow down and maybe try to sleep. I completely tore into her. I screamed until my throat was raw, told her she was small-minded, intellectually stagnant, and actively trying to sabotage my work. If anyone tried to slow me down, or if they even looked at me with that... that pitying, concerned expression, the euphoria would instantly curdle into this vicious, explosive irritability. So, yes, the elevated mood, the grandiosity, the endless talking, the rage—it all came as a package deal, and it has lasted far, far longer than a week.
Do you feel like you are currently experiencing the most severe episode of elevated mood and energy in your life?

Well, that's... that's a difficult question to answer with a simple yes or no, because "severe" is such a loaded term, isn't it? I mean, clinically speaking, we look at severity in terms of functional impairment, the presence of psychotic features, the risk of harm... but experientially, living inside it? It's much harder to quantify. 

Have I had episodes like this before? Yes, of course. I've had periods in my twenties and thirties where the engine was running too hot, where I was staying up for days, writing furious, brilliant treatises on cognitive behavioral theory that, in hindsight, were mostly just word salad. I've had times where I felt that same electric current under my skin, that same certainty that I was operating on a higher plane of existence. 

But this time... this time it feels different because of the context. The catalyst. Because Garrett is gone. The energy isn't just this spontaneous, biological upswing. It feels like it's fueled by this massive, traumatic void. So the elevation, the energy, the absolute buzzing frenzy of it all... it feels more desperate. It feels like if I stop moving, if I stop thinking, if I let the RPMs drop even a little bit, the reality of his death is going to catch up with me and completely annihilate me. 

So is it the most severe? I don't know. The grandiosity is certainly up there. The irritability is definitely at a peak—I mean, I've never screamed at my sister like that in my entire life, not even when we were teenagers. The sheer velocity of my thoughts right now is staggering. But I can't definitively say it's the *most* severe episode of my life because my baseline for comparison is so skewed right now. I'm trying to evaluate the structural integrity of a building while I'm currently standing inside it during an earthquake, you know? It's just... it's all-consuming. That's the best way I can describe it. It's completely, utterly all-consuming, whether it breaks the historical record for severity or not.
Do you feel like your current state of elevated mood and energy is interfering with your daily life or relationships?

Interfering? I... well, "interfering" is almost too mild a word for what's happening. It’s not just an interference, it’s a complete and total dismantling of my entire life.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my experience of hearing Garrett's voice, which corresponds to my symptom of hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Intellectually? Yes. I mean, as a clinician, that is exactly the textbook explanation I would offer a patient. Bereavement hallucinations. The psyche’s desperate, fascinating attempt to bridge the gap between profound attachment and sudden, unacceptable loss. I’ve read the literature, I’ve... well, I’ve counseled people through complex grief responses. So, part of me desperately wants to neatly categorize it as exactly that—a subconscious coping mechanism, a way for my brain to buffer the shock. 

But... and this is the entire crux of why I actually came in, why I finally decided I needed to sit in this chair... the experiential reality of what is happening completely defies my clinical understanding. Because I keep hearing Garrett’s voice, and it is not some vague, internal echo of a memory. It’s not an internal monologue. I hear him as clearly as if he is standing right directly behind me. 

I’ll be out on the trail, you know, just trying to burn off some of this relentless, buzzing energy, and he'll speak. Or I'll be in my painting room. That's my sanctuary, my private space where I go to focus and create, and suddenly his voice is just... occupying the actual acoustic space of the room. The timbre of it, the pitch, the slight intake of breath he always took before he made a sarcastic comment—it’s flawless. It has spatial origin. 

And it creates this agonizing cognitive dissonance. Because the rational part of my brain—the part that spent years in grad school, the part that understands object permanence and mortality—knows he’s dead. I know he is gone. But in the moment? When that sound hits my eardrums? It feels completely, absolutely real. It doesn't feel like a coping mechanism in that split second. It feels like he is physically standing there, and my brain just accepts it as reality before my logic can even attempt to catch up. It’s terrifying, frankly, to have your own sensory input override your reality testing that completely.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced any periods of significantly decreased need for sleep that lasted for several days before hearing Garrett's voice?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I only started hearing Garrett’s voice during that wired stretch when I barely slept, took on impossible projects, and felt driven to keep going. I had never heard him like that before the mood shift, and it wasn’t something that happened during ordinary grief.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the temporal relationship between the decreased need for sleep (a manic symptom) and the onset of hallucinations (hearing Garrett's voice), which aligns with the requirement that psychotic features occur exclusively during the manic episode.

patient.answer:
Well, that's... that's actually the sequence of events that finally pushed me to make this appointment, because the timing of it all is just so clinically significant. If I were charting this for a patient, I'd be circling the timeline in red ink, you know? Because, no, I didn't hear him before the sleep issues started. It wasn't just ordinary grief where you think you hear a key in the lock or a footstep on the stairs in the weeks right after the funeral. This was entirely different. 

The auditory hallucinations—and I know that's what they are, even if they feel entirely real in the moment—they only started during this... this wired stretch. That's really the best way to describe it. It was after I had gone several days with barely any sleep. I’m talking maybe two hours a night, if that, and yet I felt completely rested. More than rested, I felt driven. I was taking on these massive, impossible projects around the house, repainting the entire living room at 3 AM, reorganizing my entire clinical library by publication year and then by author’s theoretical orientation... just driven by this relentless, buzzing motor to keep going, keep moving, keep doing. 

And it was right in the middle of that—when I was running on fumes but felt like a nuclear reactor—that I first heard him. Clear as day. I had never heard him like that before this entire mood shift happened. It was only once the energy spiked, once the sleep dropped off a cliff, and once I was locked into this hyper-focused, irritable state that his voice actually manifested in the physical space of the room. So the sleep disruption definitely preceded the voice. It's like the lack of sleep and the energy surge somehow thinned the veil between my internal grief and my external sensory processing, allowing the hallucination to break through.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced any periods of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted for at least one week?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This whole crisis has been unfolding for about a month since Garrett died.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the length of time the elevated or irritable mood has lasted ('at least one week'). The patient's duration profile specifies that the crisis has been unfolding for about a month, which directly answers the timeframe queried.

patient.answer:
Well, as for the duration, yes, absolutely. It’s been far longer than a week. If we’re looking at the entire timeline of this... this whole crisis, this entire state of being wired and irritable and just vibrating with this bizarre energy, it has been unfolding for about a month now. 

It all really started tracking back to when Garrett died. That was the catalyst, obviously. The first few days after it happened, I was just numb, which is standard, of course. But then, rather than slipping into a typical depressive mourning period, the engine just turned over and started revving. And it hasn't stopped. So for the past month, I have been locked into this elevated, agitated, completely relentless state. It's not just a passing mood swing or a couple of bad days where I felt a bit snappy. It has been a sustained, unbroken month of feeling like I am operating at a hundred and fifty percent capacity, while simultaneously being so irritable that the slightest interference makes me want to tear the walls down. 

So, yes, to answer your question about the one-week criteria, we have well and truly surpassed that. It’s been a solid four weeks of this continuous, exhausting, yet somehow exhilarating escalation since I lost him. It's fascinating, really, in a horrifying sort of way, how the mind can sustain this level of physiological and psychological arousal for an entire month without just completely short-circuiting. But here I am, thirty days in, and the motor is still running hot.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's current state could be related to a bereavement-related hallucination or a manic episode by inquiring about potential feelings of guilt or self-blame
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty or blame yourself for Garrett's death?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep replaying every last conversation with Garrett and every cancelled patient session, convincing myself I failed everyone and that people would be better off if I weren’t in the way.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feelings of guilt or self-blame regarding Garrett's death, which corresponds to the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom.

patient.answer:
Guilt? Oh, God, guilt doesn't even begin to cover it. It's... it's like this crushing, suffocating weight that I just drag around with me every single second of the day. I mean, intellectually, I know the stages of grief, I know about survivor's guilt, I know how the mind tries to find control in a situation where there was none. I could give a seminar on it. But experiencing it? It's entirely different. 

I just... I keep replaying every single interaction, every last conversation with Garrett. I analyze the tone of my voice, the words I chose, the things I didn't say. Did I tell him I loved him enough that morning? Was I too distracted by work? I comb through my memories like a crime scene investigator, looking for the exact moment I failed him. And it's not just Garrett. It bleeds into everything else. I think about my patients, the ones whose sessions I've had to cancel recently because I'm in this... this state. I think about how I'm abandoning them when they need me, how I'm failing in my ethical duty as a clinician. 

It just spirals, you know? It starts with Garrett and then it just expands outward until I'm absolutely convinced that I have failed everyone who has ever relied on me. I look at the wreck I've become, this buzzing, hallucinating mess, and I genuinely, deeply believe that everyone—my patients, my colleagues, my friends—would just be so much better off if I weren't in the way. If I just... removed myself from the equation. It's this profound, inescapable sense of utter worthlessness that just sits in my chest, completely immune to any cognitive restructuring or rational thought I try to apply to it. It’s just... it’s exhausting.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced any periods of abnormally elevated mood that lasted for at least one week and were accompanied by at least three other specific symptoms such as inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, or excessive talkativeness?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: At first I felt almost lit up, like I had some urgent purpose no one else could see, but I’d snap into rage if anyone questioned me or tried to slow me down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of abnormally elevated mood, which corresponds directly to the Elevated_Irritable_Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, we are definitely checking off the diagnostic criteria today, aren't we? But yes, to answer your question about that specific cluster of symptoms... absolutely. It wasn't just that I had energy or felt a little better. At first, I felt almost... lit up. That's the best phrase for it. Incandescent. Like my brain had been plugged directly into a high-voltage line. 

I felt like I had this urgent, profound purpose that no one else could see or even begin to comprehend. I was entirely convinced I was making these groundbreaking, visionary connections about the nature of grief and human consciousness, things that were going to completely revolutionize my clinical practice and probably the entire field of psychology. I felt untouchable, honestly. My mind was just expanding to hold all these brilliant insights, and I felt so uniquely capable, so much smarter and more dialed-in than anyone around me. 

And because I was having all these massive revelations, I couldn't stop talking about them. The words were just spilling out of me, completely unspooled and rapid-fire. I was leaving these frantic, ten-minute voicemails for my colleagues in the middle of the night—because, as we established, my need for sleep was basically zero—just talking a mile a minute about my theories, jumping from one idea to the next. 

But the flip side of that elevation... the really destructive part... was how volatile it was. If anyone didn't immediately grasp my brilliance, or if they questioned me, I would just snap into absolute rage. I mean, a blinding, terrifying level of anger. My sister came over to check on me, saw the state of the house and the manicured chaos of my library project, and gently tried to suggest I slow down and maybe try to sleep. I completely tore into her. I screamed until my throat was raw, told her she was small-minded, intellectually stagnant, and actively trying to sabotage my work. If anyone tried to slow me down, or if they even looked at me with that... that pitying, concerned expression, the euphoria would instantly curdle into this vicious, explosive irritability. So, yes, the elevated mood, the grandiosity, the endless talking, the rage—it all came as a package deal, and it has lasted far, far longer than a week.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Do you feel like you are currently experiencing the most severe episode of elevated mood and energy in your life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to compare the current episode's severity to past experiences, which does not directly map to a specific symptom in the profile.

patient.answer:
Well, that's... that's a difficult question to answer with a simple yes or no, because "severe" is such a loaded term, isn't it? I mean, clinically speaking, we look at severity in terms of functional impairment, the presence of psychotic features, the risk of harm... but experientially, living inside it? It's much harder to quantify. 

Have I had episodes like this before? Yes, of course. I've had periods in my twenties and thirties where the engine was running too hot, where I was staying up for days, writing furious, brilliant treatises on cognitive behavioral theory that, in hindsight, were mostly just word salad. I've had times where I felt that same electric current under my skin, that same certainty that I was operating on a higher plane of existence. 

But this time... this time it feels different because of the context. The catalyst. Because Garrett is gone. The energy isn't just this spontaneous, biological upswing. It feels like it's fueled by this massive, traumatic void. So the elevation, the energy, the absolute buzzing frenzy of it all... it feels more desperate. It feels like if I stop moving, if I stop thinking, if I let the RPMs drop even a little bit, the reality of his death is going to catch up with me and completely annihilate me. 

So is it the most severe? I don't know. The grandiosity is certainly up there. The irritability is definitely at a peak—I mean, I've never screamed at my sister like that in my entire life, not even when we were teenagers. The sheer velocity of my thoughts right now is staggering. But I can't definitively say it's the *most* severe episode of my life because my baseline for comparison is so skewed right now. I'm trying to evaluate the structural integrity of a building while I'm currently standing inside it during an earthquake, you know? It's just... it's all-consuming. That's the best way I can describe it. It's completely, utterly all-consuming, whether it breaks the historical record for severity or not.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Do you feel like your current state of elevated mood and energy is interfering with your daily life or relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I became unable to practice safely, cancelled patient sessions, fell behind on documentation, and my wife had to call crisis services because I couldn’t trust myself alone. Being admitted to the hospital felt like the point where my work, home life, and safety had all stopped functioning.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the current state of elevated mood and energy is interfering with daily life or relationships, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Interfering? I... well, "interfering" is almost too mild a word for what's happening. It’s not just an interference, it’s a complete and total dismantling of my entire life. 

If you look at my professional life, for instance... as a clinician, I have a fundamental ethical duty to my patients. Beneficence, nonmaleficence, all of that. And I reached a point very recently where I had to look at myself and realize I became completely unable to practice safely. How could I possibly sit in a room and hold space for someone else's trauma or anxiety when I am vibrating out of my own skin? When my thoughts are moving at a thousand miles an hour? I couldn't. So I just... I started cancelling patient sessions left and right. I abandoned them. And the administrative side of my practice? Completely gone. I fell so drastically behind on my documentation—progress notes, treatment plans, billing—all of it just sitting there, piling up into this insurmountable mountain because my brain simply couldn't slow down enough to string a coherent clinical sentence together on a screen. 

And then there’s my home life. My wife... God, my poor wife. She has been trying so incredibly hard to hold the walls up while I’ve been spinning out into the stratosphere. It got to the point where this energy, this constant, relentless buzzing... it wasn't just exhausting anymore, it was actually becoming terrifying. I couldn't trust myself alone. I really couldn't. The impulses, the sheer velocity of my mind, the unpredictability of what I might do or say next... it became a genuine liability. She actually had to call crisis services. My own wife, having to call a crisis team for her husband who is supposed to be a mental health professional... do you have any idea how deeply humbling and just utterly devastating that is? 

So, yes, it is interfering. Honestly, being admitted to the hospital... walking through those doors and surrendering my shoelaces and my autonomy... it really felt like the definitive breaking point. It was the exact moment where I had to look around and accept that my work, my home life, and my own basic physical safety had all just completely stopped functioning. Everything just ground to an absolute, catastrophic halt.
